source.title: Divine Ethics - Selected Textbook Pages - 17 September 2026
source.scope: Nine focused topics from the twelve teaching pages actually supplied. The first three PDF pages are a contents list, not the full chapters. The older nineteen-page course packet remains a separately labeled background section in the review. No official exam weighting or answer key has been supplied.

pages.topic: Prayer, gratitude, trust, sincerity and planning contents
Value of time; planning and organization
Planning principles and first four characteristics
Benefactors, effects and gratitude for gratitude
Five signs of trust and the camel case
Knowledge of God, prayer and responses

limits: No title/copyright page is included. Exact book title, edition and authorship are not asserted from the contents list alone.
Piety, detailed repentance elements, levels of intention, later planning factors and social-ethics chapters appear in the contents but their full teaching pages are absent from this new extract.
Printed pages 47 and 40 end during examples. Their unseen continuations are not reconstructed.
Narrations are studied as cited by the course, not newly authenticated hadith. Spiritual outcomes are not clinical guarantees or a basis for blaming a person for illness or hardship.
These are newly authored practice MCQs. A file named Exam PDF can still contain textbook pages; neither teaching scan establishes an authentic past-paper question bank.

modules.title: Planning, organization and the value of time
modules.takeaway: Planning prepares a purposeful course of action. Organization puts it into practice at the proper time.
paragraphs: The daily bank analogy supplies 86,400 units that expire at the end of each day. Its referent is the 86,400 seconds in a day. Time is a limited opportunity for material and spiritual development, not a stock that can be carried into tomorrow. The lesson therefore connects valuing life with preparing and implementing a plan.

Planning means conceptualizing and preparing a suitable plan. Organization means implementing it. A list of goals without execution remains incomplete; activity without thoughtful priorities is not a substitute for planning. The cited letter to Malik al-Ashtar emphasizes doing each task in its proper place and time, avoiding both premature haste and laziness about tasks that can now be done.

Four planning principles are visible on printed page 60: time management, implementation, reflection, and seeking experienced advice. Time is allocated among worship/religious duties, work and obtaining life’s provisions, and permitted rest/leisure. These periods need not be equal. Their lengths depend on actual needs and priorities.

Implementation requires recognizing the suitable time, ranking tasks by priority and then acting at that time. Reflection draws on one’s own and others’ experience, considers present and future circumstances, and thinks through beginning and outcome. Good advisers combine knowledge and experience with understanding of one’s abilities; parents, competent scholars and relevant specialists are examples, not interchangeable authorities on every subject.

The first four characteristics shown are defined and prioritized goals; steps that actually serve those goals; a comprehensive plan covering responsibilities, activities and requirements; and moderation that matches capabilities with aspirations. The contents page locates additional planning material later, but those later pages were not supplied. Material and spiritual responsibilities both belong in the plan.
modules.trap: Three time categories do not mean three equal eight-hour blocks. A detailed timetable can still be a poor plan if its activities do not serve its goals.
recall: What are the four planning principles on the supplied page?
Time management, implementation, reflection, and mentors/seeking advice.
How does comprehensiveness differ from moderation?
Comprehensiveness avoids omitted responsibilities. Moderation makes the whole plan realistic relative to needs and capabilities.

modules.title: Sincerity, ostentation and dependent means
modules.takeaway: A good-looking action and a sincere intention are different questions. Using a human means does not itself mean treating it as independent of God.
paragraphs: The extract distinguishes apparent polytheism, understood in the text as acknowledging multiple gods or worshipping other beings, from hidden polytheism: verbally acknowledging one God while attributing independent efficacy to another being. The operative qualification is independence. Asking a person for help, taking a loan or using a natural means is not by itself the belief being criticized.

Ostentation means showing off through worship or apparently good deeds for worldly recognition or advantage. The examples include prayer to gain a superior’s favor or a pay rise, pilgrimage to gain respect, and helping poor people in order to attract praise. Outward correctness does not establish a pure motive. Conversely, visibility alone does not establish ostentation; the stem must give evidence about the intention.

The course describes ostentation as a form of hidden association and as harmful rather than morally neutral. Some forms are subtle and require introspection, self-purification and sustained effort to recognize and address. One should not infer a stranger’s inward motive merely from a public action.

Sincerity purifies action from non-divine motives and has degrees. The supplied conclusion presents love of God, attention to His blessings and attributes, and obedience as the way to deepen it. Printed page 57, listed under levels of intention, is not present; a complete taxonomy of those levels cannot be recovered from this scan.
comparisons: Explicitly directing divine worship elsewhere in this account
Treating another cause as independent of God
Acting for display, praise or worldly advantage
Purifying the purpose of one’s action
modules.trap: Do not confuse a public act with an act performed for publicity. Do not confuse seeking help with attributing independent divine power.
recall: Why is borrowing money not automatically hidden polytheism?
The distinction concerns belief in independent power, not the mere use of a human means.
Can an outwardly good deed have a defective motive?
Yes. The text’s examples distinguish beneficial appearance from a purpose centered on praise or advantage.

modules.title: Seven practices for cultivating sincerity
modules.takeaway: Change the intention and the habits that feed display, rather than merely changing who sees the action.
paragraphs: The seven numbered practices are: cultivate love of God; reflect on the impermanence of everything else; recognize the damage caused by ostentation; conceal worship where appropriate rather than publicize it; practice unobtrusive worship such as fasting; use meaningful remembrance, particularly la ilaha illa Allah; and recognize obedience as one’s own responsibility whose benefit returns to oneself rather than demanding reward from other people.

The first practice redirects ambition through love. The second contrasts transient human status and advantage with the enduring divine witness; the page mentions remembrance of death and graves as reminders of impermanence. The third stresses that ostentation harms the deed and the person, rather than simply adding no extra merit.

Concealing worship is an exercise against attention-seeking, not a statement that all public worship is invalid. Fasting is used as an example because others may not know of it unless told. For la ilaha illa Allah, the passage emphasizes both the meaning of divine unity and its unobtrusive recitation: it specifically notes that the lips need not meet as the tongue moves. The point is inward sincerity, not a mechanical guarantee produced by sounds.

The final practice rejects performing obligations as a transaction for praise or repayment from observers. Together these practices act on the source of motivation, the imagined value of approval and the behaviors that advertise oneself.
comparisons: Exposes display as an ethical problem
Connect attention to the purpose of action
modules.trap: Privacy can assist sincerity, but it is not a substitute for it. A concealed act can still be planned as a later story to gain praise.
recall: Name all seven practices without looking.
Love of God; impermanence; recognizing ostentation’s harm; concealing worship; fasting; meaningful la ilaha illa Allah; fulfilling duty without demanding human recompense.
Why does the source recommend fasting here?
It offers an opportunity to worship without others knowing unless the person announces it.

modules.title: Trust in God, effort and five signs
modules.takeaway: Tawakkul combines responsible effort with reliance on God. It does not make effort or natural means unnecessary.
paragraphs: Printed page 52 explicitly rejects handing over one’s responsibilities while remaining idle. The farmers who stopped farming are criticized for laziness, not praised as exemplary reliance. The source presents effort as a means of realizing capacities and developing individuals and society. Its criticism is of avoidable idleness, not a judgment on people unable to work.

The theological explanation for trust is that natural causes have capacities granted by God rather than independent power. Water, food and medicine illustrate means that should still be used. Within this account, reliance and practical action operate together. This is not an instruction to abandon evidence-based care or a guarantee that a particular medicine always works.

Five signs are listed on printed page 54: hopeful reliance on God; dignified confidence rather than subservient fear of others or difficulties; serious effort toward goals; freedom from greed and consuming preoccupation with sustenance; and peace/happiness. Reliance does not demand refusing ordinary assistance or denying one’s needs.

The camel example joins tying the camel with trust. It is an applied test of using means, not an argument for leaving the animal unsecured. The conclusion describes degrees of trust, including reliance across all affairs, and locates it in conviction in divine unity. The umbrella story on printed page 52 illustrates confidence in supplication; it is not a rule that prayer guarantees immediate rain.
comparisons: Reliance plus responsible use of means
Neglect of a responsibility excused as faith
Real means whose ability depends on God
A spiritual orientation, not proof of immunity to hardship
modules.trap: Serious effort is itself on the five-sign list. A person’s anxiety or hardship is not enough to diagnose absent faith.
recall: How do the farmers and camel examples express the same distinction?
Both reject abandoning an available practical responsibility in the name of trust.
List the five signs.
Hopeful reliance, dignified confidence, serious effort, freedom from greed/preoccupation with sustenance, and peace/happiness.

modules.title: Remembrance of the heart and the apple case
modules.takeaway: Inward awareness is central and should shape behavior even without human witnesses.
paragraphs: The teacher asks each student to eat an apple where nobody can see. The favored student returns without eating because he finds no place outside God’s awareness. The case tests sustained awareness of divine presence rather than secrecy, obedience to an unseen police officer or skill at finding a hiding place.

The conclusion identifies remembrance of the heart as the most important form and says it prepares one to benefit from practical and verbal remembrance. Heart here means inward attention and orientation, not cardiac tissue. Speech, action and inward attention are connected rather than rival alternatives.

The source associates remembrance with release from excessive worldly preoccupation, spiritual growth and tranquility. These are teachings about spiritual life, not a diagnostic test or a promise that a clinical anxiety disorder will disappear. The new scan gives this conclusion and case, not the full preceding chapter.
modules.trap: A lack of human witnesses does not remove accountability in the case. Reciting words alone is not the inward attention the conclusion prioritizes.
recall: What is the precise lesson of the uneaten apple?
Awareness of God persists where human observers are absent.
How are the three forms related?
Inward remembrance is central and supports meaningful verbal and practical expression.

modules.title: Gratitude in recognition, speech and action
modules.takeaway: Practical gratitude uses a blessing well; thanks to God do not cancel gratitude to a human benefactor.
paragraphs: The first level recognizes a blessing and appreciates its worth. The second expresses thanks verbally; al-hamdu lillah and shukran lillah are examples, especially in the prostration of thankfulness. The final, most important stage is practical thankfulness: using the blessing in a way pleasing to God. The sequence distinguishes awareness, expression and ethical use.

The concrete examples are speech used for good rather than backbiting or slander; sight kept from forbidden uses; feet not used to enter sinful settings; beauty accompanied by chastity; wealth used without waste and with help for the needy; and knowledge or a learned trade used in service. These are applications, not separate fourth or fifth levels.

God’s lack of need means that giving thanks benefits and develops the grateful person; it does not supply a deficiency in God. Recognition and words remain important, but a person who praises a blessing while misusing it has not completed practical gratitude.

Printed page 47 also discusses a human benefactor’s right: thank them, acknowledge them respectfully, pray sincerely for their good and repay kindness when able. These obligations coexist with divine gratitude. The opening of the grape-gift case contrasts contempt with appreciation; its continuation is missing, so no further ending is asserted.
comparisons: Acknowledge, pray for and reciprocate kindness when able
modules.trap: Owning resources or saying a phrase is not the same as using a blessing well. Practical gratitude does not erase respectful verbal thanks.
recall: Why is serving others with knowledge practical gratitude?
It applies the received ability in a beneficial way rather than only admiring or describing it.
What duties to a benefactor are named?
Verbal thanks, respectful acknowledgment, sincere prayer for their good and repayment when able.

modules.title: Gratitude’s effects and five obstacles
modules.takeaway: A blessing’s possession and its grateful use are distinct. Even the capacity to give thanks is treated as a further blessing.
paragraphs: The chapter associates gratitude with increased blessings and warns that ingratitude can lead to a blessing being taken away. This ethical warning is not a method of identifying why a particular person suffered a loss. The chapter then explains that the very ability to thank is another gift, so one never becomes a fully self-sufficient giver who has exhausted all reasons for gratitude. The resulting chain motivates continuing humility and thankfulness, not giving up because perfect repayment is impossible.

Five obstacles are named: failing to recognize blessings; recognizing and then forgetting them; envy of what others have; greed or dissatisfaction with one’s own share; and a generally negative outlook. Non-recognition differs from forgetting, and envy of another’s gifts differs from insatiable demand for more for oneself.

The page pairs patience in difficulty with gratitude in blessing. It distinguishes general gifts available broadly from particular spiritual gifts. Abundance by itself does not establish spiritual success: a person may misuse continued prosperity and become more heedless. The text’s warning about misuse is not permission to infer a stranger’s moral standing from wealth or poverty.

The cited reminder that few servants are grateful is identified on printed page 49 as Quran 34:13. It supports attentiveness rather than a numerical estimate of good people. The conclusion joins heartfelt and practical thanks.
comparisons: Once noticed, no longer attended to
Habitual failure to see good across life
modules.trap: Increase in possessions is not an automatic certificate of gratitude or divine approval. Do not reverse the source’s ethical teaching into a judgment of someone’s circumstances.
recall: What are all five obstacles?
Non-recognition, forgetting, envy, greed/dissatisfaction and a negative outlook.
Why thank God for being thankful?
The source treats the ability and opportunity to express gratitude as a further blessing.

modules.title: Prayer, effort and a wise response
modules.takeaway: Supplication expresses dependence and accompanies striving. An answer is not defined solely by receiving the exact object requested.
paragraphs: The page connects prayer with knowledge of God as the source of perfection and material and spiritual benefits. The person presents needs to God and strives toward the objective. Reliance does not remove effort. Attaining a goal may deepen faith, while non-attainment need not destroy hope in divine goodness.

Five effects are listed: remembrance and proximity to God with His love; protection from possible difficulties; rescue from enemies; increased sustenance; and purification from sins. Study them as the course’s spiritual teaching, not a guarantee of a specified outcome on demand. Quran 25:77 and 40:60 are cited in the page’s introductory panel.

The account of an answer emphasizes wisdom. A response may come through ordinary material means or extraordinary means. A person asking for relief from poverty may not become rich; the page discusses both absent effort and the possibility that the requested outcome would be harmful. These are possible explanations in the teaching, not grounds for claiming knowledge of why a particular person suffers.

The mother-and-knife analogy shows why refusing the exact object can express care rather than indifference. The scan ends before the example finishes, so only the visible contrast is used. Detailed etiquette, recommended times/places and further discussion appear in the older packet or in contents headings, not on this new page.
comparisons: Use available means toward the goal
May differ from the requested object
Does not by itself identify wrongdoing or rejection
modules.trap: “My precise request was not fulfilled” does not logically establish “God did not respond” within this account.
recall: List the five effects named here.
Remembrance/proximity/love; protection; rescue from enemies; increased sustenance; purification from sins.
What does the knife analogy illustrate?
A requested object can be withheld for the recipient’s good.

modules.title: Immediate repentance, habits and moral development
modules.takeaway: Prompt correction interrupts the growth of harmful habits. Delay is risky both because habits deepen and because future time is uncertain.
paragraphs: The extract urges repentance at the first opportunity. Repeated wrong actions can become entrenched habits that affect conduct and disposition, making later rectification more difficult. The second argument is uncertainty about how much life remains: an intention to repent later does not ensure the opportunity will remain.

The illness-and-medicine comparison is a moral metaphor: sin damages the soul and repentance counters it. It is not a medical diagnosis or a treatment claim. The page places the opportunity for repentance in earthly life, stating that its door closes at death and afterward. The discussion also explains why small, sustained good actions may develop a person more effectively than an impressive act that is immediately abandoned.

The passage attributed to Murtaza Mutahhari likens earthly moral development to fruit ripening while attached to its tree. Once detached, the opportunity for that kind of growth ends. The further point is that regret after seeing inevitable consequences is not the same as a free inward moral transformation during life.

This supplied page argues for immediacy; it does not supply the complete elements of repentance or a list distinguishing minor and major sins. Those appear in contents headings but their detailed pages are absent. Do not invent their contents or treat postponement as harmless simply because repentance is emphasized.
comparisons: Allows habit to deepen and risks losing the opportunity
Begins correction while change remains possible
Forms and reinforces a constructive disposition
Illustrates the limited period for moral development
modules.trap: Difficulty in changing a habit is an argument to begin sooner, not evidence that change during life is impossible.
recall: What are the two reasons against delay?
Wrongdoing can become habitual, and the time available before death is uncertain.
Why is post-consequence regret distinguished from repentance here?
The passage contrasts compelled reaction to visible consequences with inward moral transformation during earthly life.
